title: The AI Skills Gap Is a Judgment Gap
author: Joel Salinas
summary: AI strategy coach Joel Salinas uses a new DataCamp/YouGov survey of 517 enterprise leaders to argue that the widely-discussed AI skills gap is actually a judgment gap. The survey found that 77% of organizations already offer AI training and most leaders believe in AI's ROI potential, yet only 21% report significant returns -- a figure that roughly doubles to 42% among organizations with a mature, company-wide upskilling program. Every specific capability gap leaders named -- turning information into decisions, communicating with it, applying it to real work, knowing what to trust -- was a judgment problem wearing a skills label, not a technical deficiency, which is why sending everyone the same ten-minute training video fails. Salinas frames this partly through his own decision to turn down a client who wanted a tool recommendation without examining how their people actually think about AI. He closes with five free diagnostic questions leaders can ask before buying anything, while also flagging DataCamp's own commercial interest in the report's training-focused conclusion.
points: A 2026 DataCamp/YouGov survey of 517 enterprise leaders found 77% already offer AI training, yet only 21% report significant returns -- rising to 42% among organizations with a mature, company-wide upskilling program.

Every capability gap leaders named -- interpretation, trust, decision-making, application -- was a judgment problem, not a technical-skill problem, despite most organizations still running access-focused training.
The chess analogy captures the core critique: teaching how a tool's pieces move is not the same as teaching someone to play, i.e. to exercise judgment under real conditions.
The author's five-question audit costs nothing and diagnoses the real gap before any tool purchase.
quotes: A 2026 DataCamp and YouGov survey of 517 enterprise leaders found that most organizations already offer AI training, yet every capability gap those leaders named was about interpretation, trust, and decision-making rather than technical skill.

You can teach somebody how every piece on a chessboard moves in about ten minutes, and by the end they'll tell you the bishop goes diagonally and the knight does that odd L-shape. None of it makes them able to play.
Without strong foundations, advanced tools (from dashboards and BI to AI systems) increase confidence without increasing correctness, which amplifies risk rather than reducing it.

When people are unsure how outputs are governed, DataCamp found, they "either over-rely on outputs or avoid using tools altogether." Both are judgment failures, and both look like adoption on a dashboard.
Only 35% have a mature, organization-wide upskilling program. 77% already offer some kind of AI training, so access isn't the gap.
DataCamp sells AI upskilling, so a report concluding that AI training drives returns is also their sales pitch. That doesn't make it false, but it earns a harder look.
